docs.title: The Official LEDGER Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to the official documentation for the Linked Environmental Data and Greenhouse Emissions Resource (LEDGER). LEDGER is a data utility to make analysis of emission data easier. At its core is a database that stores emission data for nation states, administrative 1 levels, and cities. The data is harmonized from various sources. Analysis of the data is provided via a REST API and a high-level Python client that abstracts away the API. The ultimate goal is to focus on the science instead of munging data.

We hope this documentation helps you get started quickly and makes exploring the LEDGER database easier and more productive.

LEDGER is a community-driven project and we highly value your feedback and contributions:

docs.title: ledgerdata.Client.Client dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: Base

LEDGER Data Cient

Source code in ledgerdata/Client.py 
@dataclass
class Client(Base):
    """LEDGER Data Cient"""

    # Limit concurrency to 10 requests at once, adjust as needed
    _sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)

    def actors(
        self,
    ) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """retreive actor emissions

        Args:
            actor_id (str|List[str]): code for actor your want to retrieve

        Returns:
            DataFrame: data for each emissions dataset
        """
        return pd.DataFrame(Actors().actors())

    def emissions(
        self,
        actor_id: str,
    ) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """retreive actor emissions

        Args:
            actor_id (str|List[str]): code for actor your want to retrieve

        Returns:
            DataFrame: data for each emissions dataset
        """
        return pd.DataFrame(Emissions().emissions(actor_id=actor_id))

    def emissions_raw(
        self,
        actor_id: str,
    ) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """retreive actor emissions raw

        Args:
            actor_id (str|List[str]): code for actor your want to retrieve

        Returns:
            DataFrame: data for each emissions dataset
        """
        return Emissions().emissions(actor_id=actor_id)

    def targets(self, actor_id: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """retreive actor targets

        Args:
            actor_id (str|List[str]): code for actor your want to retrieve

        Returns:
            DataFrame: dataframe of targets
        """
        return pd.DataFrame(Targets().targets(actor_id=actor_id))

    def population(self, actor_id: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """retreive actor population

        Args:
            actor_id (str|List[str]): code for actor your want to retrieve
            ignore_warnings (bool): ignore warning messages

        Returns:
            DataFrame: dataframe of population
        """
        return pd.DataFrame(Population().population(actor_id=actor_id))

    def gdp(self, actor_id: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """retreive actor gdp

        Args:
            actor_id (str|List[str]): code for actor your want to retrieve
            ignore_warnings (bool): ignore warning messages

        Returns:
            DataFrame: dataframe of gdp
        """
        return pd.DataFrame(GDP().fetch(actor_id=actor_id))

    def parts(
        self, actor_id: str, part_type: Optional[str] = None, *args, **kwargs
    ) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """retreive actor parts

        returns subnational, cities, companies, etc. within an actor_id

        Args:
            actor_id (str|List[str]): code for actor your want to retrieve
            part_type (str): retrieve actors from administrative part ['planet', 'country', 'adm1', 'adm2', 'city', 'organization', 'site']

        Returns:
            DataFrame: dataframe of actors parts
        """
        return pd.DataFrame(Actors().parts(actor_id=actor_id, type=part_type))

    async def emissions_async(self, actor_id: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
        data = await Emissions().emissions_async(actor_id=actor_id)
        return pd.DataFrame(data)

    async def _emissions_with_sem(self, actor_id: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
        async with self._sem:
            return await self.emissions_async(actor_id)

    async def emissions_many(self, actor_ids: List[str]) -> List[pd.DataFrame]:
        tasks = [self._emissions_with_sem(actor_id) for actor_id in actor_ids]
        return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    # sync wrappers that run the async code in an event loop
    def emissions_sync(self, actor_id: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
        return asyncio.run(self.emissions_async(actor_id))

    def emissions_many_sync(self, actor_ids: List[str]) -> List[pd.DataFrame]:
        return asyncio.run(self.emissions_many(actor_ids))

docs.title: Database Architecture
docs.text: PostgreSQL is used as the database management system. The database models and schema are defined using the SQLModel object-relational mapper, while Alembic manages database schema migrations. This approach of keeping everything in the Python ecosystem makes the project easier to maintain.

docs.title: Entity Relationship Diagram
docs.text: The following entity-relationship diagram (ERD) shows how the tables are structured and how they interact from a high level.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
The schema follows the following design principles:

  • Singular table names. (e.g. "Actor" not "Actors")
  • Compound primary keys. For many tables, there are compound primary keys; that is, keys with multiple columns that are unique across the table. When the table is referenced as a foreign key in many places, however, we use a single constructed identifier, which makes references simpler.
  • Provenance information provided: We make a strong effort to include a datasource_id for rows that provides data provenance.
  • Timestamps Most rows in table include a created_at and updated_at timestamp column. These mark when the data was imported or updated in the database, which helps with synchronisation and delivery over the Web. Publication of the datasource can be found in the DataSource table.
  • Consistent units imported data sets may have varying units. When the data is pre-processed the units may be changed to match the database schema. For instance, emissions in LEDGER are provided in tonnes of gas for all records.
  • Multiple sources of truth. We track multiple records of the same information for emissions data to facilitate the intercomparison of methodologies. However, we only track a single source of truth for contextual data such as population, GDP, energy consumption, and emission targets.
  • Constructed identifier Identifiers are often constructed by the data importer to be unique. A common pattern is to use a colon ':' to separate parts of an identifier that are unique. For example, datasource_id values are often composed of the publisher ID and a unique ID for the publication.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
The RESTful API is created with FastAPI and psycopg and is provides low-level access to the database. The API (and database) is currently hosted with DigitalOcean. This REST API is mainly intended for web applications to query the database. If you are using LEDGER for data analysis we suggest using the Python Client.

Here, we provide a brief overview of the API endpoints. The table below summarizes the LEDGER API endpoints used to query actors and associated datasets. {actor_id} denotes a path parameter representing the unique identifier of an actor (e.g., country, state, province, or city) in the LEDGER database. Countries, states, and provinces use ISO3 codes, while cities use LOCODE.

Endpoint Description Query Parameters /actor List all actors in the database. — /actor/{actor_id}/parts List actors contained within another actor (e.g., states within a country). type /actor/{actor_id}/gdp Return GDP time series for a given actor. — /actor/{actor_id}/population Return population time series for a given actor. — /actor/{actor_id}/energy_consumption Return energy consumption time series for a given actor. — /actor/{actor_id}/targets Return emissions reduction targets associated with an actor. — /actor/{actor_id}/emissions Return greenhouse gas emissions time series. Results can be filtered by gas species, sector classification, or datasource. datasourcesectorgas /sector returns emission sectors taxonomycode /gwp returns global warming potential assessment_reportgastime_horizon /datasource returns global warming potential namepublisher

For complete documentation please see the API documentation in ReDOC and Swagger format below.

docs.title: Table Details
docs.text:
The models are grouped into the following areas:

  • Actors and sources: geographic entities and external data sources
  • Sectors and global warming potential: classification and conversion data
  • Emissions and targets: emissions records, totals, and climate targets
  • Contextual data: GDP, population, and energy-consumption data

class DataSource(SQLModel, table=True):
    """Data source table

    Attributes:
        id: Unique identifier 
        name: name of the data source
        publisher: publisher of the data source
        published_date: date data set was published
        version: data source version
        url: URL data source was downloaded from
        created_at: date record was created
        updated_at: date record was last updated
    """
    id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    name: str
    publisher: Optional[str]
    published_date: Optional[datetime]
    version: Optional[str]
    url: Optional[str]
    created_at: Optional[datetime] = Field(
        sa_column=Column(
            TIMESTAMP(timezone=True),
            nullable=False,
            server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
        )
    )
    updated_at: Optional[datetime] = Field(
        sa_column=Column(
            TIMESTAMP(timezone=True),
            nullable=False,
            server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
            server_onupdate=FetchedValue(),
        )
    )

class Actor(SQLModel, table=True):
    """Represents a geographic or political entity.

    Attributes:
        id: Unique identifier for the actor.
        name: Human-readable name of the actor. 

            - For countries, use the
              [ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code](https://www.iso.org/obp/ui/#iso:pub:PUB500001:en).
            - For subnational regions, such as states and provinces, use the
              [ISO 3166-2 code](https://www.iso.org/obp/ui/#iso:pub:PUB500002:en).
            - For cities, use the
              [UN/LOCODE](https://unece.org/trade/cefact/unlocode-code-list-country).

        is_part_of: ID of the parent actor, if applicable. (e.g. US-NY is_part_of US)
        type: Geographic or political type of the actor.
        datasource_id: ID of the source providing the actor data.
    """
    id: str = Field(primary_key=True)
    name: str
    is_part_of: Optional[str] = Field(default=None, foreign_key="actor.id")
    type: ActorType
    sovereign_code: Optional[str] = Field(default=None, foreign_key="actor.id")
    datasource_id: Optional[str] = Field(foreign_key="datasource.id")
    created_at: Optional[datetime] = Field(
        sa_column=Column(
            TIMESTAMP(timezone=True),
            nullable=False,
            server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
        )
    )
    updated_at: Optional[datetime] = Field(
        sa_column=Column(
            TIMESTAMP(timezone=True),
            nullable=False,
            server_default=text("CURRENT_TIMESTAMP"),
            server_onupdate=FetchedValue(),
        )
    )

class GWP(SQLModel, table=True):
    """Global Warming Potential

    Attributes:
        id: Unique identifier for this GWP record.
        gwp: Global warming potential value.
        time_horizon: Time horizon of the GWP, in years.
        gas: Gas for which the GWP is reported. See
            [GasType][models.GasType] for the supported gases.
        assessment_report: Assessment report used for the GWP value.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
LEDGER currently provides two main ways to access data: a REST API and Python client. We suggest starting with ledgerdata, a Python package that provides a high-level access to the REST API.

This getting started page will walk you through the steps to start using ledgerdata.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: ledgerdata can be installed via uv or pip. We recommend uv.

docs.title: UV recommended
docs.text: uv add ledgerdata

docs.title: pip
docs.text:
pip install ledgerdata

Now you can start using ledgerdata in your projects!

docs.title: First instanatiate a client object
docs.text:
The client object provides access to methods that make it easy to query the LEDGER database. First, import the Client class from ledgerdata and instantiate an object:

The client object lets you query the LEDGER database. First, import Client() and then create an object:

from ledgerdata import Client

client = Client()

You can then use the client’s methods to query the database with a pattern like this client.method().

Next we will walk you through some of the ways you can query the database to retrieve data.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
Actors refers to any:

  • adm0: nation
  • adm1: state / province
  • adm2: city

docs.title: List all actors
docs.text:
The following will return a dataframe with all the actors in the database:

df_actors = client.get_all_actors()

docs.title: Parts of an actor
docs.text:
sometimes you want parts of an actor 

df_parts = client.parts(actor_id="US")

docs.title: Retrieve contextual data
docs.text:
Once you know the ids of the actors you are interested in you can easily retrieve contexual data on the actor. Keep in mind that not all contexual data is available for each actor.

Note

unlike emissions, we only provide one datasource for each actor.

docs.title: Emission targets
docs.text:
list_of_ids=["CA", "US", "GB"]

df = client.targets(actor_id=list_of_ids)

docs.title: Population
docs.text:
list_of_ids=["CA", "US", "GB"]

df = client.population(actor_id=list_of_ids)

docs.title: GDP
docs.text:
list_of_ids=["CA", "US", "GB"]

df = client.gdp(actor_id=list_of_ids)

docs.title: Energy Consumption
docs.text:
list_of_ids=["CA", "US", "GB"]

df = client.energy_consumption(actor_id=list_of_ids)

docs.title: Emissions
docs.text: Where possible, emissions are broken down into subsector and gas and aggregated using global warming potentials (GWP).

docs.title: Total emissions
docs.text:
list_of_actors = ["CA", "US", "GB"]

df = client.emissions_total(actor_id=list_of_actors)

docs.title: Decompose emissions
docs.text:
You can retrieve emissions based on gas and sectors

params = {
    actor_id: "CA",
    gas: "CH4",
    sector: "agriculture"
}

df = client.emissions_by(**params)

docs.title: Global Warming Potentials
docs.text:
You can retrieve global warming potentials from an assessement report

df = client.gwp(assessment_report="AR5")
